chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Abu Abdullah al-Razi, from al-Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Amr, from al-Khalaf ibn Hammad, from al-Mahraz, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Debt (al-dayn) is of three types: A man who, when he is owed money, grants time (to the debtor), and when he owes money, pays it back and does not delay; this is for his benefit and not against him. And a man who, when he is owed money, demands full payment, and when he owes money, pays in full; this is neither for him nor against him. And a man who, when he is owed money, demands full payment, but when he owes money, delays; this is against him and not for his benefit.
ai.seo_question: What are the three types of debtors described in Shia hadith regarding financial ethics?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq categorizes these three approaches in *Al-Khisal* to illustrate the spiritual consequences of financial conduct, linking the first to divine reward, the second to neutrality, and the third to spiritual loss. This hadith emphasizes that ethical flexibility in lending (granting time) combined with diligence in repaying is the ideal state, while rigidity in both or negligence in one leads to diminished spiritual standing. The classification serves as a practical guide for Muslims to navigate commercial transactions with both justice and generosity.
